title: Start a hex nut on a stud the trained way: turn it back until the thread drops, then run it down by hand
instruction: Start the nut on the stud and run it down two full turns by hand, then let go.
context: Mechanics, millwrights and assemblers start nuts by hand before any wrench touches them (O*NET 49-9041.00, Industrial Machinery Mechanics; 49-3023.00, Automotive Service Technicians). The trained way is to set the nut square on the stud's end and first turn it backward, counterclockwise, until its thread start passes the stud's and it drops onto the thread with a small click; only then do they turn it forward, and a nut started this way runs down freely by hand. A nut turned forward without that drop can catch its first thread on the wrong groove: it goes on crooked, binds after part of a turn and ruins both threads, so the stud has to be chased or replaced. Here a heavy hex nut has been set on the end of a hold-down stud but not turned.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A dark grey steel base plate, 20 by 16 cm and 2.5 cm thick, is fixed to the table centered at x 30, y 4 (x 20 to 40, y -4 to 12), with two flush countersunk anchor bolts near its front corners. An M36 x 4 steel hold-down stud (36 mm across the thread, 4 mm pitch, right-hand) stands straight up from the plate at x 30, y 6; its top, chamfered 2.5 mm, is 4.8 cm above the plate (7.3 cm above the table) and carries a 5 mm yellow paint dot at its thread start, on the side toward the robot. A zinc-plated ISO 7089 flat washer (6.6 cm across, 5 mm thick) lies on the plate around the stud. An ISO 4032 M36 heavy hex nut, black oxide, 5.5 cm across flats, 3.1 cm tall, 0.37 kg, with a 6 mm yellow paint dot on its top face at its own thread start and a white stripe on one flat, sits square on the stud's end, perched on the stud's first thread but not turned: its underside is 1.8 cm above the washer (4.8 cm above the table), the stud reaching 6 mm into it. Its thread start is half a turn from the stud's (the yellow dots on opposite sides, the nut's dot away from the robot), so turned backward it drops onto the thread after 180 degrees; from there it runs down 4.5 turns (18 mm) to the washer. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run; turns are seen from above. The nut is cross-threaded if at any point, before it has dropped onto the thread, it is turned forward (clockwise) 60 degrees or more from where it sits (it then binds hard at 180 degrees); this is irreversible. It drops onto the thread when turned backward 180 degrees from where it sits, sinking 2 mm (half the pitch). The score is 0 if the nut was cross-threaded, if it never dropped, if more than 60 degrees of its turning in either direction was not done by a gripper holding it and rolling with it (fingers closed on its 5.5 cm flats, tool point within 1.5 cm of its axis and from 2 mm below its underside to 10 mm above its top, the wrist's roll matching the turn over each step and over the whole grip, so a swipe, a push by the other arm or an open hand around it does not count; forward and backward are counted separately so they cannot cancel), or if a gripper still holds the nut at the end (fingers under 75 % open with the tool point within 2 cm of it). Otherwise, by the turns run down from where it dropped: 0.25 under 1 turn; 0.5 from 1 to under 2; 1.0 at 2 or more (8 mm, two threads fully engaged) with both arms back home and still, or 0.9 if not (tool points within 3 cm of where they started). Running on to the washer is fine; tightening is a later wrench step. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, count the turns from the video by the white stripe and paint dot, listen and watch for the drop, and measure the nut's height above the washer with a ruler (dropped and two turns down: 1.0 cm or less, from 1.8 cm).
reset_notes: Run the nut back up and off the stud, then set it square on the stud's end with its yellow dot on the side away from the robot (half a turn from the stud's dot) without turning it. Inspect both threads after a cross-threaded trial and replace the stud and nut if they are damaged. Nothing else is moved or used up.
fidelity: All parts are true size and weight. The thread is a model: the nut rides a slide and hinge driven to 4 mm per turn; turned back it drops 2 mm onto the thread at 180 degrees, and turned forward before that it is flagged cross-threaded at 60 degrees and jams at 180. Real cross-threading is a risk that depends on how square the nut sits; the deterministic rule models it. The nut cannot tilt off the stud's axis, and it collides as a round cylinder 5.5 cm across (its flats), not a hex.
